# NOTES


# Pre-processing
```{r}
library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(writexl)
library(tidytext)

brown_occupations <- read_excel("C:/Users/alpko/OneDrive/Belgeler/Green Brown/Dictionaries/onet_brown_occupations.xlsx")
task_statements <- read_excel("C:/Users/alpko/OneDrive/Belgeler/Green Brown/Dictionaries/onet2020_task_statements.xlsx")

# Standardization
brown_tasks <- brown_occupations %>%
  mutate(
    soc_code_clean = str_trim(as.character(`O*NET-SOC Code`))
  )

task_statements <- task_statements %>%
  mutate(
    soc_code_clean = str_trim(as.character(`O*NET-SOC Code`)),
    soc_code_clean = str_remove(soc_code_clean, "\\.\\d+$")
  )

# Selecting brown tasks
brown_task_statements_full <- task_statements %>%
  semi_join(
    brown_tasks %>% distinct(soc_code_clean),
    by = "soc_code_clean"
  ) %>%
  select(-soc_code_clean)

nrow(brown_task_statements_full)
head(brown_task_statements_full)
n_distinct(brown_task_statements_full$`O*NET-SOC Code`) # 88, Vona et al. (2018)

write_xlsx(
  brown_task_statements_full,
  "brown_task_statements_full_rows.xlsx"
)
```
There are 85 unique broad occupations, but 88 occupations if the more detailed occupations are also included (n = 4). I choose to include them as well. 

# Frequency Analysis
```{r}
# Loading task descriptions for brown occupations
brown_task_statements <- read_excel(
  "brown_task_statements_full_rows.xlsx"
)

# Counting individual words in the task statements
word_frequencies <- brown_task_statements %>%
  filter(!is.na(Task)) %>%
  select(Task) %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, Task) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>%
  filter(str_detect(word, "[a-z]")) %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE)

# Displaying the 300 most frequent words
top_300_words <- word_frequencies %>%
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = 300, with_ties = FALSE)

print(top_300_words, n = 300)

# Plotting the 20 most frequent words
top_20_words <- word_frequencies %>%
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = 20, with_ties = FALSE)

ggplot2::ggplot(
  top_20_words,
  ggplot2::aes(x = reorder(word, n), y = n)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_col() +
  ggplot2::coord_flip() +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Most Frequent Words in Brown-Occupation Task Statements",
    x = "Word",
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()

# Exporting all word frequencies to Excel
write_xlsx(
  word_frequencies,
  "brown_task_word_frequencies.xlsx"
)
```
Because the vast majority of these words are not meaningful by themselves and may express very common tasks in brown and non-brown jobs, I decided to conduct distinctive words analysis, which provides words that are most commonly found in the task descriptions of the brown jobs. To reiterate, these brown jobs are those that were identified by Vona et al. (2018)

# Distinctive Words (Unigram) Analysis
```{r}
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Identifying brown and non-brown occupations
brown_codes <- brown_occupations %>%
  mutate(
    soc_code_clean = str_remove(
      str_trim(as.character(`O*NET-SOC Code`)),
      "\\.\\d+$"
    )
  ) %>%
  distinct(soc_code_clean)

all_tasks <- task_statements %>%
  mutate(
    task_id = row_number(),
    soc_code_clean = str_remove(
      str_trim(as.character(`O*NET-SOC Code`)),
      "\\.\\d+$"
    ),
    group = if_else(
      soc_code_clean %in% brown_codes$soc_code_clean,
      "brown",
      "other"
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Task), str_trim(Task) != "")

# Checking the size of each group
all_tasks %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(
    n_occupations = n_distinct(soc_code_clean),
    n_task_statements = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Tokenizing all task statements
task_words <- all_tasks %>%
  select(task_id, group, Task) %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, Task) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>%
  filter(str_detect(word, "[a-z]"))

# Counting each word only once per task statement
task_word_presence <- task_words %>%
  distinct(task_id, group, word)

word_counts <- task_word_presence %>%
  count(group, word, name = "tasks_with_word") %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = group,
    values_from = tasks_with_word,
    values_fill = 0
  )

# Calculating the proportion of task statements containing each word
brown_total <- sum(all_tasks$group == "brown")
other_total <- sum(all_tasks$group == "other")

distinctive_words <- word_counts %>%
  mutate(
    brown_prevalence = brown / brown_total,
    other_prevalence = other / other_total,
    difference = brown_prevalence - other_prevalence,
    prevalence_ratio = if_else(
      other_prevalence > 0,
      brown_prevalence / other_prevalence,
      NA_real_
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(difference))

# Displaying the 300 most distinctive words
top_300_distinctive <- distinctive_words %>%
  filter(brown >= 5) %>% # excluding bigrams appearing less than 5
  slice_max(
    order_by = difference,
    n = 300,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) %>%
  select(
    word,
    brown,
    other,
    brown_prevalence,
    other_prevalence,
    difference,
    prevalence_ratio
  )

print(top_300_distinctive, n = 300)

# Plotting the 20 most distinctive words
top_20_distinctive <- distinctive_words %>%
  filter(brown >= 5) %>% 
  slice_max(
    order_by = difference,
    n = 20,
    with_ties = FALSE
  )

ggplot(
  top_20_distinctive,
  aes(x = reorder(word, difference), y = difference)
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Words Most Distinctive of Brown Occupations",
    x = "Word",
    y = "Difference in task-statement prevalence"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Exporting the results
write_xlsx(
  list(
    All_words = distinctive_words,
    Top_300_distinctive = top_300_distinctive
  ),
  "brown_distinctive_word_analysis.xlsx"
)
```
Above, I identify the top 300 most distinctive words in brown task descriptions. They are identified by selecting the words that have the most prevalence differences. For each word, brown prevalence is calculated by dividing the number of brown task descriptions that include the word by the number of all brown task statements (n = 1661). Non-brown (other) prevalence is similarly calculated by dividing number of non-brown task descriptions that include the word by the number of all non-brown task statements. Then, the difference in prevalence becomes brown prevalence minus non-brown prevalence, which I multiply by 100 to express it in percentage points. The top 300 most distinctive words in brown task descriptions is found by ranking words according to this difference calculation. The positively larger the difference, the higher the keyword is ranked.

However, it is not very reliable to extract dictionary keywords from this list, either. Nevertheless, in the following chunk, I decided to try finding more dictionary terms by identifying the most commonly found two-word (bigram) and three-word (trigram) phrases in the task statements of brown jobs. 

# Distinctive N-gram Analysis
```{r}
# Tokenization and removing stopwords
clean_task_words <- all_tasks %>%
  select(task_id, group, Task) %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, Task) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>%
  filter(str_detect(word, "[a-z]"))

# Reconstructing the cleaned text for each task statement
clean_tasks <- clean_task_words %>%
  group_by(task_id, group) %>%
  summarise(
    Task_clean = paste(word, collapse = " "),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Keeping the original task counts as denominators
brown_total <- sum(all_tasks$group == "brown")
other_total <- sum(all_tasks$group == "other")

# Bigrams
bigram_presence <- clean_tasks %>%
  unnest_tokens(
    bigram,
    Task_clean,
    token = "ngrams",
    n = 2
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(bigram)) %>%
  distinct(task_id, group, bigram)

bigram_counts <- bigram_presence %>%
  count(group, bigram, name = "tasks_with_phrase") %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = group,
    values_from = tasks_with_phrase,
    values_fill = 0
  )

bigram_distinctive <- bigram_counts %>%
  mutate(
    brown_prevalence = brown / brown_total,
    other_prevalence = other / other_total,
    difference_pp = (brown_prevalence - other_prevalence) * 100,
    prevalence_ratio = if_else(
      other_prevalence > 0,
      brown_prevalence / other_prevalence,
      NA_real_
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(difference_pp))

top_300_bigrams <- bigram_distinctive %>%
  filter(brown >= 5) %>% 
  slice_max(
    order_by = difference_pp,
    n = 300,
    with_ties = FALSE
  )

print(top_300_bigrams, n = 300)

# Trigrams
trigram_presence <- clean_tasks %>%
  unnest_tokens(
    trigram,
    Task_clean,
    token = "ngrams",
    n = 3
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(trigram)) %>%
  distinct(task_id, group, trigram)

trigram_counts <- trigram_presence %>%
  count(group, trigram, name = "tasks_with_phrase") %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = group,
    values_from = tasks_with_phrase,
    values_fill = 0
  )

trigram_distinctive <- trigram_counts %>%
  mutate(
    brown_prevalence = brown / brown_total,
    other_prevalence = other / other_total,
    difference_pp = (brown_prevalence - other_prevalence) * 100,
    prevalence_ratio = if_else(
      other_prevalence > 0,
      brown_prevalence / other_prevalence,
      NA_real_
    )
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(difference_pp))

top_300_trigrams <- trigram_distinctive %>%
  filter(brown >= 5) %>%
  slice_max(
    order_by = difference_pp,
    n = 300,
    with_ties = FALSE
  )

print(top_300_trigrams, n = 300)

# Plotting the 20 most distinctive bigrams
top_20_bigrams <- bigram_distinctive %>%
  filter(brown >= 5) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = difference_pp, n = 20, with_ties = FALSE)

ggplot(
  top_20_bigrams,
  aes(x = reorder(bigram, difference_pp), y = difference_pp)
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Most Distinctive Two-Word Phrases",
    x = "Bigram",
    y = "Prevalence difference (percentage points)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Plotting the 20 most distinctive trigrams
top_20_trigrams <- trigram_distinctive %>%
  filter(brown >= 5) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = difference_pp, n = 20, with_ties = FALSE)

ggplot(
  top_20_trigrams,
  aes(x = reorder(trigram, difference_pp), y = difference_pp)
) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Most Distinctive Three-Word Phrases",
    x = "Trigram",
    y = "Prevalence difference (percentage points)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Exporting results to Excel
write_xlsx(
  list(
    Bigrams_all = bigram_distinctive,
    Bigrams_top300 = top_300_bigrams,
    Trigrams_all = trigram_distinctive,
    Trigrams_top300 = top_300_trigrams
  ),
  "brown_tasks_ngram.xlsx"
)

```
I followed the same logic I applied to the Distinctive Words (Unigrams) Analysis section. This was also not very helpful, especially for trigrams. I could not derive enough number of phrases to complete my dictionary. I now decided to manually look at the task statements of every brown occupation of the ONET 25.0 (2020) data.
